extracted.intended_audience: USCIS/DHS adjudicators, immigration attorneys, advocates, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for how DHS/USCIS will evaluate whether an alien is likely to become a public charge, including the health, family, assets/resources, and financial-status factors and the types of evidence to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health — medical examination requirement and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most immigrant visa applicants applying with DOS and those applying for adjustment of status with USCIS are required to submit a medical examination. Nonimmigrants generally are not, except certain categories; consular or CBP officers may require exams if there are concerns about inadmissibility on health grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would consider immigration medical examinations submitted with the application and any medical condition information in the totality of the circumstances. The presence or absence of a medical condition is a factor only insofar as it pertains to the alien’s likelihood of becoming a public charge (e.g., ability to care for self, attend school, or work). Absence of a diagnosis is a positive factor. DHS recognizes some conditions are treatable and may not be determinative. Applicants may submit additional medical records or related information to clarify conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class A medical conditions (health-related inadmissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Class A medical conditions (as defined in HHS regulations) make an alien inadmissible on health-related grounds unless a waiver is available and authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class A conditions include: communicable disease of public health significance (e.g., gonorrhea, infectious Hansen’s disease, infectious-stage syphilis, active tuberculosis); failure to meet vaccination requirements; present or past physical or mental disorders with associated harmful behavior or harmful behavior likely to recur; and drug abuse or addiction. HHS/CDC definitions and Technical Instructions govern classification. DHS may consider Class A conditions as part of the public charge determination but they are not the sole factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician reporting requirements for Class A and Class B conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: HHS regulations direct physicians conducting immigration medical examinations to explain specific elements on the medical report/notification when identifying Class A or Class B conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Class A: explain 'the nature and extent of the abnormality; the degree to which the alien is incapable of normal physical activity; and the extent to which the condition is remediable . . . [and] the likelihood, that because of the condition, the applicant will require extensive medical care or institutionalization.' For Class B: report the degree to which the alien is incapable of normal physical activity, the extent to which the condition is remediable, and the likelihood the applicant will require extensive medical care or institutionalization. Physicians must follow CDC Technical Instructions (see 42 CFR 34.3(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class B medical conditions (reporting and relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Class B medical condition is a physical or mental condition, disease, or disability serious in degree or permanent in nature; it does not make an alien inadmissible on health-related grounds but is relevant to the public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CDC Technical Instructions describe Class B as a departure from normal health that may interfere with self-care, school, or work, or may require extensive future treatment or institutionalization. When identified, physicians must report nature/severity, impact on ability to work/attend school/support self, and whether hospitalization/institutionalization will be required. DHS will consider Class B conditions in the totality of the circumstances and will not treat them as sole determinative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability — consideration within the health factor
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would consider disability only to the extent that the disability, in the context of the alien’s individual circumstances, impacts the likelihood of the alien becoming a public charge (frequently whether it affects ability to work, attend school, or support self).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes protections under the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, IDEA, and related laws; disability cannot be the sole basis for inadmissibility. Under the totality of the circumstances framework, a disability is treated as any other medical condition: considered alongside mandatory factors and any required affidavit of support. DHS notes employer reasonable-accommodation requirements and other protections but also focuses on practical effects of disability on self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s family status is a factor in determining likelihood of becoming a public charge: DHS proposes to consider whether the alien has a household to support, is being supported by another household, and whether household size makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS would view family status often in connection with assets/resources because larger households generally require more resources. DHS would consider household size as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(d). A child who is part of a parent’s household is assessed as part of that larger household; household size alone will never dictate outcome and may be offset by positive factors (e.g., sufficient income or access to assets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status — threshold and formula
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS must consider an applicant’s assets, resources, and financial status as part of the totality of the circumstances to assess likelihood of future public benefit receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes using a gross household income threshold of at least 125 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) based on household size as a positive indicator. If household income is less than 125% FPG, household assets and resources should equal at least five times the difference between household income and 125% FPG. Household liabilities (e.g., from credit reports) are part of financial status. DHS requests comments on whether 125% FPG is appropriate and provides an example calculation (household of 4 with $24,000 income would need $36,875 in assets to bridge the $7,375 gap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of assets and resources (types of evidence USCIS will consider)
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS would consider specified kinds of documentary evidence when reviewing assets and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: the alien’s annual gross household income (all sources before deductions, excluding public benefits); additional income from individuals not included in household who physically reside and whose income will be relied upon; continuing additional income from other persons/sources (most recent calendar year), excluding public benefits; household cash assets as reflected in checking/savings statements in the last 12 months; household non-cash assets convertible to cash within 12 months (net cash value of real estate minus loans/ liens, annuities, securities, retirement and educational accounts, and other easily-convertible assets). DHS states 'All of this information is potentially relevant to a determination of the alien’s assets and resources.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of financial status (types of evidence USCIS will consider)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing liabilities or past reliance on public benefits, DHS proposes to review specific evidence relating to financial status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS would consider: evidence that the alien has applied for or received any public benefit (as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b)) on or after the effective date; evidence of certification/approval to receive public benefits on or after the effective date; evidence the alien applied for or received a fee waiver for immigration benefits after the effective date; credit histories and credit scores; and whether the alien has private health insurance or financial resources to pay for medical costs associated with medical conditions identified in 8 CFR 212.22(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Current or past receipt/application for public benefits as a negative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Current or past applications for or receipt of public benefits (as defined in the proposed rule) suggests the alien's overall financial status is weak and may indicate they will receive benefits in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to consider any current and past receipt or application for public benefits as a negative factor in the totality of the circumstances because it is indicative of weak financial status. The weight given to this factor is context-dependent and part of the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances principle
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will use a totality of the circumstances framework when making public charge inadmissibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All mandatory factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education/skills) and the affidavit of support (if required), along with any other submitted evidence, must be weighed together; no single factor will automatically determine the outcome. DHS will assess positive and negative factors in context (e.g., treat disability or medical conditions as part of health factor, consider treatability and supporting evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of additional medical records and attestations to clarify conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would take into consideration any additional medical records or related information provided by the alien to clarify any medical condition included on the medical form or other information that may outweigh negative factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such documentation may include a licensed doctor's attestation of prognosis and treatment of a medical condition. DHS notes that additional evidence demonstrating treatability or ability to work/attend school may mitigate negative weight of a medical diagnosis in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver availability and remission (health-related inadmissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A waiver of the health-related ground of inadmissibility is available for certain Class A conditions; drug abuse/addiction is not waivable except where addiction is found to be in remission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waivers are available for communicable diseases of public health significance, physical or mental disorder accompanied by harmful behavior, and lack of vaccinations (see INA section 212(g)(1)). For drug abuse or addiction, a waiver is unavailable for inadmissibility due to current addiction, but an applicant may overcome inadmissibility if drug abuse/addiction is found to be in remission (CDC Technical Instructions reference: 'Remission'). DHS may still consider such conditions in the public charge analysis even if inadmissibility is addressed separately.
